analysis.one_liner: Requires car makers to share repair information with owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee — it was introduced in June 2002 with two sponsors and died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern cars rely on computers, and car makers can lock repair information behind access codes that only their franchised dealers can unlock. This bill would have required manufacturers to disclose to owners and independent repair shops everything needed to diagnose, service, and repair a vehicle, with the Federal Trade Commission writing the rules and both owners and shops able to sue to enforce them. It would also have created an FTC process to protect genuine trade secrets, so manufacturers could not use that label to hide repair information they already share with dealers.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle owners, who would get competitive prices and more repair choices instead of being steered back to dealers for computer-related repairs; independent repair shops, which would gain access to the same diagnostic information dealers use; and the aftermarket parts industry, which the bill's own findings say employs over 5 million workers and generates roughly $200 billion in annual sales [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers would have to provide owners and repair facilities with the information needed to diagnose, service, or repair a vehicle, including codes to integrate replacement equipment [S2].
The FTC would write uniform disclosure rules within 180 days, with information delivered in writing or on the Internet, applying to vehicles made after model year 1994 [S2].

A failure to disclose would count as an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act, and vehicle owners or repair shops could sue in federal court to stop violations and recover attorney and expert witness fees [S2].

The bill shields genuine trade secrets from public disclosure — but not from a manufacturer if it already gives the same information to franchised dealers or other repair facilities, closing the loophole of dealer-only access [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers and their franchised dealer networks, which would lose the advantage of being the only shops able to fix computer-controlled problems, and which would bear the cost of preparing and distributing repair documentation.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would carry real compliance costs to document, standardize, and publish repair information for every model, and the bill's rulemaking would have to draw a line between repair information and genuinely protected trade secrets [S3].

Opponents could argue that opening access to emissions-control diagnostics risks tampering that worsens pollution; the bill acknowledges this concern by barring the FTC from issuing rules that interfere with the EPA's authority over emissions-control diagnostic systems [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer case was strong: as cars became computerized, control of diagnostic codes was quietly shifting repair work from the shop of the owner's choice to the manufacturer's dealers, raising prices and limiting choice. The bill anticipated the main objection by carving out trade secrets and protecting EPA emissions authority. The cost falls on automakers and dealers, who would surrender a captive service revenue stream — a cost to them, and lower repair prices for car owners.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2002 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the Congress ended with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone introduced the bill on June 13, 2002, with Senator Mark Dayton as cosponsor — just two senators total [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill was never taken up again [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and their franchised dealer networks are better off: they kept exclusive control of computerized repair information, and independent shops and car owners never got the access the bill would have guaranteed.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Sen. Mark Dayton
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only other Senate supporter.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill died in committee before any vote, so no roll calls show where the parties stood; its two supporters were both Minnesota Democrats.

industries.note: Dealers' advantage came from exclusive access to computer diagnostic information and access codes; the bill would have ended that exclusivity by forcing manufacturers to share the same information with owners and independent shops. Note that the industry never had to state its position on the record — the bill died in committee without a hearing.

Shops would gain access to the diagnostic and repair information needed to fix modern computerized cars, letting them compete with dealers for the same work. Their gain comes directly out of dealers' captive repair revenue.

The bill's findings cite an aftermarket industry of over 5 million workers and about $200 billion in annual sales, which would benefit from owners being free to choose original or aftermarket parts. Wider repair competition increases demand for aftermarket parts.
